title: Gen Z: the myth of life experience November 3, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: Unlocked Graduates, which recruits graduates into two-year prison officer roles in England and Wales, uses a decade of programme data to challenge the claim that young Gen Z officers lack the life experience for the job. About four in five of its participants are Gen Z, and the youngest start at 21. Independent Ministry of Justice analysis found Unlocked officers were 18 percentage points more likely to still be in post after two years than officers from mainstream routes. Participants of every age recorded a similar number of achievements, and the only age effect ran the other way, with older participants more likely to leave. The authors argue that the life experience refrain stands in for a low recruitment bar, poor training and acceptable ageism, and that prisoners' preference for older officers reflects affinity bias. Their recommendation is to raise the quality threshold at entry and train properly, and not to raise the minimum age.
points: Officers recruited through Unlocked, 80 percent of whom are Gen Z, were 18 percentage points more likely to be in the role after two years than mainstream recruits.
Across age groups, participants recorded similar performance, and the one age effect was that older participants were more likely to withdraw.
The demand for life experience is argued to stand in for a low recruitment bar, poor training and a culture where ageism is more acceptable than other discrimination.
Preferences for older officers likely reflect affinity bias, while prisoners in practice value relational skill and careful use of authority, which can be selected for and trained.
The remedy is to assess the capabilities that predict performance and hold all joiners to a higher standard, not to raise the minimum age.
quotes: If age explains performance, it becomes acceptable to leave officers under-trained, under-supported and under-invested in, and then blame their youth when things go wrong.

Independent MoJ analysis found that officers recruited through Unlocked, 80% of whom are Gen Z, are 18 percentage points more likely to be in the role after two years than officers entering through mainstream routes.

Across our programme data, participants of every age group recorded a similar average number of “achievements” in their first two years. Given the right training and support, Gen Z matched their older colleagues.
We think it stands in for three things: a low bar at recruitment, poor training, and a culture in which ageism is more acceptable than other kinds of discrimination.
Some people arrive with years of life experience and none of the skills the job needs. Others arrive young and ready.
Those are skills you can select for and train. Having children is not.
Prisons don’t have a young-officer problem. They have a selection and training problem, and age is the easiest thing to blame.
A higher bar may screen out more young applicants. But it screens them out for the right reason, and it leaves a wider pool to choose from than an age cut-off would.
